title: Brain-wide omission responses did not habituate when 58 mice met image omissions for the first time; their power rose with firing rate in each session and reset on day 2 (Allen VBN)
abstract: Mice in the Allen Visual Behavior Neuropixels (VBN) data set see image omissions for the first time on recording day 1 and again on day 2. We asked if the brain-wide spiking at an omitted image is a surprise response that becomes smaller with exposure. We used 60 mice with both days (117 usable active-block sessions, 85,359 good units) and only omissions with no lick from -0.25 to +0.50 s. The response was the rate change from 250 ms before the expected onset to 50-300 ms after it; its unbiased power was averaged over units of five region classes. We compared the first and the last 30 omissions of each day, with matched image flashes as control and a bootstrap over mice. The plan was written before the analysis. Results: no class showed a decrease within day 1. Omission power increased by 72% in visual cortex (log ratio +0.54, 95% CI +0.35 to +0.73) and by 81% in LGd + LP, together with a 7-64% rise of firing rate; after rate normalisation the rise was +36% in visual cortex and absent in thalamus and midbrain. At the start of day 2, omission power was equal to that at the start of day 1 (all units log ratio -0.07, -0.29 to +0.17) and lower than at the end of day 1 (-0.60), and it rose again within day 2. Rate-normalised image-flash power fell within each day (all units -0.45 on day 1), so the omission/flash ratio rose 1.9-fold. Omission activity grew smoothly towards the next image, without a step at the expected onset. Hippocampal omission power was near zero (0.4% of 11,101 units significant), so the pre-registered hippocampal habituation test was not informative. Exploratory: omissions did not cause licks, but omissions inside lick bouts gave 5-6 times larger hippocampal and midbrain responses. Conclusion: VBN omission responses follow session state, not the novelty of omissions. Limitations: exposure and session time are separated only by the day-2 reset; day 2 used novel images; only the active block was read; optotagged classes were not separated.

display.caption: Responses in bins of 15 lick-free omissions over the active block (blue: day 1, first omissions ever; green: day 2). Omission response power rises within each session with the pre-onset firing rate and starts again from the same level on day 2; the image-flash response does not rise. Bands: 95% mouse bootstrap.

Time course of the trial-reliable rate change from the pre-onset window (root of unbiased power, 50 ms bins). Omission activity grows smoothly towards the next image (+0.75 s) without a step at the expected onset; the hippocampal formation shows almost no omission response.

citations.reason: Allen Visual Behavior Neuropixels NWB files and project metadata (public S3 bucket visual-behavior-neuropixels-data) are the data of this study.

Nitzan et al. 2025 described omission responses in the same data. We confirm ramp-like cortical activity but did not detect hippocampal step responses in lick-free omissions, and show that lick-bout omissions inflate non-visual responses.
